mainTopic: Is a woman who remarried by mistake excused because 'what could she have done?' (מאי הוה לה למיעבד), and why רב פפא did not rely on it in practice
overview: This amud continues the discussion of a woman who remarried by mistake. רבינא explains that a ברייתא's labels 'deliberate' and 'accidental' are only about whether she brings a קרבן. A second answer says that ברייתא follows the רבנן and rereads its exception clause. Then עולא, רב שימי בר אשי, אביי, רבא, רב אשי and רבינא each bring a source where a woman who remarried in good faith still gets all the penalties. Each time they ask: why not excuse her with 'what could she have done?' Each time the גמרא answers that she could have avoided the mistake, either by waiting or by having the גט read. רב פפא wanted to rule leniently based on this excuse. רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע told him not to rely on so many answers, and רב פפא held back. Finally, רב אשי says we ignore a rumor, and the גמרא begins asking which rumor he means. That discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבינא: The Comparison Is Only About Bringing an Offering
steps.stepSummary: רבינא explains that the ברייתא's 'deliberate' and 'accidental' labels refer only to whether she brings a קרבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: the ברייתא is talking about a קרבן. If the court acted on its own ruling, it is like a deliberate sin, so she brings no קרבן. If she married based on witnesses, it is like an accidental sin, so she brings a קרבן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the difficulty that רב ששת raised. He says the ברייתא's words 'like deliberate' and 'like accidental' are only about whether she must bring a קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difficulty came from reading 'like a deliberate sin' as if she were fully guilty. רבינא limits those labels to קרבן law. When a person follows a court's ruling, the person brings no קרבן. When she relied on witnesses, she brings a regular חטאת for an accidental sin. So the ברייתא says nothing against the idea that she was helpless.

keyTerms.meaning: An offering brought in the בית המקדש, here a חטאת for an accidental sin
A ruling or instruction given by בית דין
A deliberate, knowing sin
An accidental, unknowing sin
Based on the testimony of witnesses

steps.confusionAlert: 'Like a deliberate sin' here does NOT mean she sinned on purpose. It only means that, like a deliberate sinner, she does not bring a קרבן. The reason is that she followed the court.

phrases.english: Ravina said,
it is taught regarding an offering:
if the court acted on their own ruling —
it is like a deliberate sin of a man with a woman,
and she does not bring an offering.
If based on witnesses —
it is like an accidental sin of a man with a woman,
and she brings an offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty raised earlier on the daf against רב ששת's 'what could she have done' idea.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope: the ברייתא's labels apply only to קרבן law.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The labels 'deliberate' and 'accidental' were taken to describe how guilty she is in general.
steps.terutzMaskana: The labels only decide whether she brings a קרבן. Following a court means no קרבן, and relying on witnesses means a קרבן.

steps.title: Second Answer: The First ברייתא Follows the Rabbis
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the first ברייתא follows the רבנן, and its exception clause is read to include two cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say: the first ברייתא follows the רבנן. Read it this way: 'except for a married woman, and one who remarried by the court's permission.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer to the same difficulty. It says the first ברייתא follows the רבנן and adjusts how its exception clause is read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן hold that a woman who remarried based on witnesses is still forbidden to her husband. So the ברייתא is not following רב ששת's 'what could she have done' approach at all. The exception clause is read to cover two cases that still need a גט: a married woman who remarried through witnesses, and one who remarried through בית דין.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you wish, say' – introduces another answer
The majority of the Sages, against a single named תנא
'And answer it like this' – explain the text with this reading
A married woman

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
this first one is the opinion of the Rabbis,
phrases.notes: 'First one' is the earlier ברייתא saying the forbidden women do not need a גט.

phrases.english: and answer it like this:
except for a married woman,
and one who married by the court's permission.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא קַמַּיְיתָא רַבָּנַן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, separate answer to the same difficulty that רבינא answered.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning the ברייתא to a different opinion (the רבנן) and adjusting its wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first ברייתא seemed to follow the view that witnesses excuse her, which is what רב ששת's difficulty was built on.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא follows the רבנן. Both the witnesses case and the court case need a גט.
steps.whatToRemember: Two answers push off רב ששת's difficulty. רבינא says the 'deliberate/accidental' labels are only about a קרבן. The other answer says the first ברייתא follows the רבנן, with a reworded exception.

steps.title: עולא Objects from a משנה About a Flawed גט
steps.stepSummary: עולא challenges 'what could she have done' using the משנה about a גט with a wrong date or place.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא objected: Do we really say 'what could she have done'? We learned in a משנה: if he dated the גט by an improper kingdom, by Media, by Greece, by the building of the Temple, or by its destruction, or if he was in the east and wrote 'west', or in the west and wrote 'east', she must leave both men, and all these penalties apply to her.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא questions רב ששת's idea of excusing a woman who 'couldn't have known.' He brings a משנה about a woman who remarried using a flawed גט. That משנה gives her the full penalties, so he is setting up the question of why she is not excused.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the גט case, the woman also had no idea anything was wrong. She simply trusted the גט. Yet the משנה makes her leave both husbands and suffer every penalty. That seems to show we do NOT excuse a woman with 'what could she have done.'

keyTerms.meaning: 'What could she have done?' – she had no way to avoid it, so she was helpless
A kingdom that is not proper, meaning one not ruling where they live
She must leave both men, the first husband and the second

phrases.english: Ulla objected:

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן מַאי הֲוָה לַהּ לְמִיעְבַּד?
phrases.english: Do we say, "What could she have done?"
But didn't we learn:
if he wrote it dated by a kingdom that is not proper,
phrases.notes: This is about the date written in the גט, counted by the years of a king.

phrases.english: by the kingdom of Media,
by the kingdom of Greece,
by the building of the Temple, by the destruction of the Temple,
if he was in the east and wrote "in the west,"
in the west and wrote "in the east" —
she must leave this one and that one,
and all these consequences apply to her.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב עוּלָּא: מִי אָמְרִינַן מַאי הֲוָה לַהּ לְמִיעְבַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new attack, this time on the basic 'what could she have done' reasoning itself.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's reasoning that a woman who couldn't have known is excused.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A woman with a flawed גט also could not have known, yet the משנה gives her full penalties. So 'what could she have done' is not accepted.

steps.title: Why Not Excuse Her Too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out the question: why don't we say 'what could she have done' in the גט case?
steps.simpleTranslation: But why? Let us say: what could she have done!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts עולא's point into a sharp question. If we excuse a helpless woman, we should excuse this one too, so why doesn't the משנה do that?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This step makes the contradiction clear. The question only works if the גט woman really was as helpless as the woman who relied on witnesses. The next step will show she was not.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But why?'
'Let us say'

phrases.english: But why?
Let us say: What could she have done!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַמַּאי? לֵימָא: מַאי הֲוָה לַהּ לְמִיעְבַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the משנה quoted in step 3 into a direct question against 'what could she have done.'
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling of the גט משנה, if 'what could she have done' is true.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If being helpless excuses her, the גט woman should be excused. But the משנה punishes her fully.

steps.title: She Should Have Had the גט Checked
steps.stepSummary: Answer: the woman with the flawed גט was not helpless. She could have had it read by an expert.
steps.simpleTranslation: She should have had the גט read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the גט case is different. She could have avoided the mistake by having someone knowledgeable read the גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'What could she have done' only applies when there truly was nothing she could do. With a גט, a scholar reading it would have caught the wrong date or place. Since she skipped a step she could have taken, she is not excused, and רב ששת's idea still stands for the witnesses case.

keyTerms.meaning: 'She should have'
To have something read by someone else
The גט, the bill of divorce

steps.whatToRemember: 'What could she have done' excuses a woman only when she had no way to check. A woman with a flawed גט could have had it read, so she is not excused and gets all the penalties.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the limit of the 'helpless' excuse. Relying on witnesses can count as helpless. Failing to check something you could have checked does not.

phrases.english: She should have had the bill of divorce read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers עולא's question by showing the גט case is different.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Telling the cases apart: in the גט case she could have avoided the mistake.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The גט woman was just as helpless as the woman who relied on witnesses.
steps.terutzMaskana: She was not helpless, since she could have had the גט read. So the 'what could she have done' excuse does not apply to her.

steps.title: רב שימי בר אשי: the צרה who remarried when the יבמה turned out to be an איילונית
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר אשי brings a case where a צרה remarried, thinking she was free. The יבמה turned out to be an איילונית, so the צרה is punished with all the penalties. Why don't we say 'what could she have done?'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר אשי said: Come and hear. A man married his יבמה, and her צרה (the other widow) went and married someone else. Then the יבמה turned out to be an איילונית. The צרה must leave both men, and all the penalties apply to her. But why? Let us say: what could she have done?
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי בר אשי brings a new case to challenge the idea that 'what could she have done?' protects a woman who remarried by mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An איילונית was never eligible for יבום, so the יבם's marriage to her did not free the צרה. The צרה acted in good faith, yet she still gets every penalty. That seems to contradict the excuse 'what could she have done?'.

keyTerms.meaning: His יבמה: his brother's widow, whom he marries through יבום
Her צרה: another wife of the same dead husband
A woman who never developed physically and cannot have children. Her marriage was a mistake, so she is not part of יבום at all
She must leave this one and that one: she loses both men
What could she have done? The argument that she was helpless and should not be punished

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי, תָּא שְׁמַע:
phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi said: Come and hear:
One who married his yevama,
and her rival wife went and married someone else,
and this one (the yevama) turned out to be an aylonit:
she must leave this one and that one,
phrases.notes: This one and that one means her new husband and the יבם. She can stay with neither.

phrases.english: and all these penalties apply to her.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַמַּאי? נֵימָא: מַאי הֲוָה לַהּ לְמִיעְבַּד?
phrases.english: But why? Let us say: what could she have done?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי, תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After עולא's challenge from the גט was answered, a new challenge is brought from a different case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The excuse 'what could she have done?'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A צרה who remarried in good faith still gets every penalty, so being helpless does not seem to protect a woman.

steps.title: She should have waited
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the צרה was not helpless. She should have waited until it was clear the יבמה was not an איילונית.
steps.simpleTranslation: She should have waited.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off רב שימי בר אשי's challenge: this woman could have done something.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whether the יבמה is an איילונית can become clear over time. The צרה rushed to remarry instead of waiting, so the excuse 'what could she have done?' does not fit her.

keyTerms.meaning: She should have: it was her responsibility
To wait

phrases.english: She should have waited.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the case does not fit: the woman was not truly helpless
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The צרה had no way to know, so the penalty contradicts 'what could she have done?'
steps.terutzMaskana: She could have waited, so she was careless, and the penalty is fair.

steps.title: אביי: the צרות of the עריות who remarried
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings a similar case. The צרות of the עריות remarried, and then the ערוה turned out to be an איילונית. They get all the penalties. Why not say 'what could she have done?'
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Come and hear. All the עריות that the חכמים said free their צרות from יבום: if the צרות went and remarried, and then the ערוה turned out to be an איילונית, the צרה must leave both men, and all the penalties apply to her. But why? Let us say: what could she have done?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי brings another case to challenge the excuse 'what could she have done?'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, when one widow is an ערוה to the יבם, her צרות are freed too. But an איילונית does not count, so here the צרות were never freed and they really needed יבום. They remarried in good faith and still get every penalty.

keyTerms.meaning: Women forbidden to a man as close relatives
They free their צרות from יבום and חליצה

phrases.english: Abaye said: Come and hear:
All forbidden relatives about whom they said
that they free their rival wives,
phrases.notes: This is the rule from the start of מסכת יבמות. If one widow is forbidden to the יבם, her צרות are freed too.

phrases.english: if the rival wives went and remarried
and these (the forbidden women) turned out to be aylonit:
she must leave this one and that one,
and all these penalties apply to her.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַמַּאי? נֵימָא: מַאי הֲוָה לַהּ לְמִיעְבַּד?
phrases.english: But why? Let us say: what could she have done?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel challenge, built on the same איילונית problem as Step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The excuse 'what could she have done?'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The צרות relied on a well-known rule and remarried in good faith, yet they are fully penalized.

steps.title: Here too, she should have waited
steps.stepSummary: The same answer: the צרה should have waited until it was clear the ערוה was not an איילונית.
steps.simpleTranslation: She should have waited.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off אביי's challenge with the same answer it gave רב שימי בר אשי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here too, whether the ערוה is an איילונית would have become clear with time. The צרה was not helpless, she was hasty, so she gets no protection.

phrases.english: She should have waited.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 8, just as Step 7 answered Step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the case does not fit: the woman was not truly helpless
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The צרה relied on the standard rule and could not have known.
steps.terutzMaskana: She could have waited, so the penalty does not contradict 'what could she have done?'.

steps.title: רבא: the scribe who mixed up the גט and the receipt
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings a case where the scribe swapped the גט and the receipt, so no divorce ever took place. If the woman remarried, she gets all the penalties. Why not say 'what could she have done?'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Come and hear. A scribe wrote a גט for the man and a receipt for the woman. He made a mistake and gave the גט to the woman and the receipt to the man, and they handed them to each other. Later it turns out the גט is in the man's hands and the receipt is in the woman's hands. She must leave both men, and all the penalties apply to her. But why? Let us say: what could she have done?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings a fourth case to challenge the excuse 'what could she have done?'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the mistake was made by the scribe, not the woman. She received what she thought was her גט, but it was really the receipt, so she was never divorced. Even so, she gets every penalty, which seems to show that being an innocent victim does not help.

keyTerms.meaning: A scribe who writes documents
A receipt. Here, the woman's written confirmation that she was paid her כתובה
And he made a mistake
Comes out from the hands of: is found in someone's possession

phrases.english: Rava said: Come and hear:
A scribe wrote a bill of divorce for the man
and a receipt for the woman,
phrases.notes: The plan was a swap: he gives her the גט, and she gives him a receipt saying she was paid her כתובה.

phrases.english: and he made a mistake and gave the bill of divorce to the woman
and the receipt to the man,
and they gave them to each other, this one to that one and that one to this one,
and after some time

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי הַגֵּט יוֹצֵא מִתַּחַת יְדֵי הָאִישׁ,
phrases.english: the bill of divorce turns up in the man's possession,
and the receipt in the woman's possession:
she must leave this one and that one,
and all these penalties apply to her.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַמַּאי? נֵימָא: מַאי הֲוָה לַהּ לְמֶיעְבַּד!
phrases.english: But why? Let us say: what could she have done!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fourth challenge, now from a case about mixed-up documents instead of an איילונית.
steps.kashyaTarget: The excuse 'what could she have done?'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The mistake was entirely the scribe's, yet she still gets every penalty.

steps.title: She should have had the גט read
steps.stepSummary: The answer: she was not helpless. She should have had the document read, and she would have seen it was a receipt and not a גט.
steps.simpleTranslation: She should have had the גט read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off רבא's challenge: she could have checked the document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like the answer to עולא in Step 5, the woman could have had someone read the document. That would have shown it was not a גט. Since she could have avoided the mistake, the excuse 'what could she have done?' does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: To have it read: to have someone read the document
The גט, the bill of divorce

steps.whatToRemember: The challenges so far (עולא, רב שימי בר אשי, אביי, רבא) all fail for the same reason: in each case the woman could have prevented the mistake, either by waiting or by having the גט read. Two more challenges of the same kind come next.

phrases.english: She should have had the bill of divorce read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 10, using the same idea as Step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the case does not fit: the woman was not truly helpless
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The scribe made the mistake, so the woman could not have known.
steps.terutzMaskana: She could have had the document read and found the mistake, so she is responsible.

steps.title: רב אשי's case: a גט with changed names
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי brings a teaching: if the husband changed names in the גט and she remarried, she gets all the penalties. Why not excuse her with 'what could she have done?'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Come and hear. If he wrote his name, her name, his city's name or her city's name differently in the גט, and she remarried, she must leave both men, and all the penalties apply to her. But why? Let us say: what could she have done!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי adds another source to the list of challenges. In this source, a woman who acted in good faith is still punished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גט with wrong names is not valid, so she is still married to her first husband. She had no idea and remarried. If 'what could she have done?' were a real excuse, she should be let off. Yet the teaching gives her every penalty.

keyTerms.meaning: he changed (wrote differently)
she must leave both this husband and that one
'these ways', meaning the full list of penalties
what could she have done? (she was helpless)

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: Come and hear:
If he changed his name or her name,
phrases.notes: He means the names as they are written inside the גט.

phrases.english: the name of his city or the name of her city
she must leave this one and that one,
and all these penalties apply to her.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַמַּאי? נֵימָא: מַאי הֲוָה לַהּ לְמִיעְבַּד!
phrases.english: But why? Let us say: what could she have done!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fifth challenge in the same pattern as אביי's and רבא's.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that 'what could she have done?' excuses her.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The woman was innocent, yet she gets full penalties. So being helpless is not accepted as an excuse.

steps.title: She should have had the גט read
steps.stepSummary: The answer: she was not helpless. Reading the גט would have shown the wrong names.
steps.simpleTranslation: She should have had the גט read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same kind of answer it gave to רבא's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mistake was right there in the written text. Someone who knows how to read a גט would have caught it. Since she could have checked, she is not considered helpless.

keyTerms.meaning: she should have
to have it read (by someone who knows)
the גט, the bill of divorce

phrases.english: She should have had the bill of divorce read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the case is not one of real helplessness
steps.terutzHavaAmina: She could not have known that the names were wrong.
steps.terutzMaskana: She could have found out by having the גט read, so 'what could she have done?' does not apply.

steps.title: רבינא's case: a 'bald' גט
steps.stepSummary: רבינא brings a case where she remarried based on a 'bald' גט, which is invalid. She still leaves both men.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: Come and hear. If a man married her based on a 'bald' גט, she must leave this one and that one, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא brings one more source against 'what could she have done?'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גט קרח is a folded, sewn-up גט that does not have enough witnesses signed on it, so it does not work. She thought she was divorced and remarried, yet she gets all the penalties. That again seems to reject the helplessness excuse.

keyTerms.meaning: he married her
a 'bald' גט: a folded גט missing some of the witnesses it needs

phrases.english: Ravina said: Come and hear:
If he married her based on a 'bald' bill of divorce,
phrases.notes: A folded גט needs a witness for each fold. When some are missing, it is called 'bald' and it does not work.

phrases.english: she must leave this one and that one, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' stands for the rest of the line: all the penalties apply, so why not say 'what could she have done?'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A sixth challenge in the same pattern.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that 'what could she have done?' excuses her.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: She trusted a גט that looked fine, yet she is fully penalized.

steps.title: Again, she should have had the גט read
steps.stepSummary: The same answer: someone who knows would have seen that the גט was missing witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: She should have had the גט read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the same answer for רבינא's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The missing witnesses could be seen on the document itself. Since checking was possible, not checking counts as her own carelessness, not as being forced by circumstances.
steps.whatToRemember: In every source brought, the woman could have checked, either by waiting or by having the גט read. So the גמרא always answers that she was not truly helpless.

phrases.english: She should have had the bill of divorce read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the case is not one of real helplessness
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The flaw in the גט could not be noticed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Someone who knows would have seen the problem, so she could have avoided it.

steps.title: רב פפא wanted to rule using 'what could she have done?'
steps.stepSummary: A story: רב פפא planned to rule leniently in a real case based on this reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא thought to rule in a real case based on 'what could she have done?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now moves from theory to a story about practical הלכה. This line sets up the objection that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since every source had been answered, רב פפא felt the argument was still standing. He was ready to treat a woman who truly could not have checked as helpless, and so free of the penalties.

keyTerms.meaning: he thought, he intended
to act in a real case (an actual ruling)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa thought to make a practical ruling
based on 'what could she have done.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After all the challenges are answered, a real ruling is attempted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב פפא intended to excuse a woman who truly could not have checked.

steps.title: רב הונא objects: all these sources go against it
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע points to the whole list of sources as reason not to rule this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע said to רב פפא: But all these teachings were taught (against it)!
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא's plan is challenged by a colleague.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not bring a new source. Instead, he points to the whole collection of sources together, all of which seem to reject the excuse.

keyTerms.meaning: these teachings (the sources brought above)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְרַב פָּפָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said to Rav Pappa:
But all these teachings were taught!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's plan to rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: So many sources point against the excuse that it should not be used.

steps.title: רב פפא: we answered them all
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says each source was explained as a case where she could have checked.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: But didn't we answer them?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא defends himself. Every source was already answered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In each case we showed she could have waited or had the גט read. So the sources only teach about cases where checking was possible, and they leave room for a case where she truly could not check.

keyTerms.meaning: we answered them (resolved the difficulty)

phrases.english: He said to him: But didn't we answer them!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב הונא's objection.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing back to the answers already given
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sources reject the excuse completely.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sources only deal with cases where she could have checked.

steps.title: רב הונא: you can't rely on answers alone
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says that a ruling should not rest on a stack of answers, because so many challenges are a warning sign.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Shall we stand and rely on answers?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא rejects רב פפא's defense. He does not say the answers are wrong; he says they are not strong enough to rule on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each answer may be possible on its own. But needing an answer for every single source suggests the excuse is not really accepted. That is too weak to act on.

keyTerms.meaning: on answers (explanations made up to deflect a challenge)
shall we stand
and rely

steps.confusionAlert: רב הונא is not proving the answers wrong. His point is that answers which are only possible are not enough to build a practical ruling on.

phrases.english: He said to him: And shall we stand and rely on answers!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב פפא's defense.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the answers as a basis for a real ruling.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A pile of answers that are only possible is too weak to act on against so many sources.

steps.title: רב פפא stopped
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא held back and did not give the lenient ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he stopped.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends: רב פפא accepted the objection and did not rule leniently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In practice, 'what could she have done?' is not used to excuse her. A woman who remarries by mistake still gets the penalties.

keyTerms.meaning: and he stopped (held back)

steps.whatToRemember: The excuse 'what could she have done?' survives every challenge on paper, but it is not used in practice. The sources against it are too many to rely on answers alone.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a rule of thumb for practical rulings: when an idea needs a forced answer for source after source, you do not act on it.

phrases.english: (And he stopped.)
phrases.notes: Some versions have this word and some leave it out. It means רב פפא held back from ruling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The result of רב הונא's rejection.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב פפא did not rule leniently. 'What could she have done?' is not relied on in practice.

steps.title: We do not worry about a rumor
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי rules that a rumor does not concern us.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: And we are not concerned about a rumor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new short ruling from רב אשי: a rumor that the husband is alive is not something we take into account.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is about the woman in the משנה who was allowed to remarry because she was told her husband died. רב אשי says an unproven rumor that he is still alive does not change anything. He does not say which rumor he means, and the next steps ask exactly that.

keyTerms.meaning: A rumor; literally 'a voice', talk going around with no real witnesses
We are not concerned; we do not take it into account

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
And we are not concerned about a rumor.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי, וּלְקָלָא לָא חָיְישִׁינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the רב פפא story ends, looking at the משנה's case from another angle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An unproven rumor that the husband is alive is ignored.

steps.title: Which rumor does he mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of rumor רב אשי is talking about.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which rumor?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question: which rumor did רב אשי mean? This sets up the options that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A rumor could start at different times, for example before or after the woman remarried. The timing could matter, so the גמרא needs to pin down what רב אשי meant.

keyTerms.meaning: Which?

phrases.english: Which rumor?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the exact case behind רב אשי's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of rumor (when it started) is meant by רב אשי's ruling.

steps.title: A rumor after marriage? He already said that
steps.stepSummary: If he means a rumor after her new marriage, רב אשי would be repeating himself, since he already said that once.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say he means a rumor after the marriage, רב אשי already said this once, as רב אשי said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the first possibility, a rumor after she remarried, and objects that רב אשי already said that rule elsewhere. It then begins quoting his earlier statement, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is repetition: a sage would not need to state the same rule twice. So this first reading seems wrong, which pushes the גמרא toward a different kind of rumor. The quote itself is only introduced here; it continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say; introduces a first suggestion that will be challenged
Marriage; here, her marriage to the second man
One time; once already

phrases.english: If we say it means a rumor that came after the marriage,

phrases.aramaic: הָא אַמְרַהּ רַב אָשֵׁי חֲדָא זִימְנָא,
phrases.english: Rav Ashi already said this once,
as Rav Ashi said:

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא קָלָא דְּבָתַר נִשּׂוּאִין הָא אַמְרַהּ רַב אָשֵׁי חֲדָא זִימְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first answer to the question 'which rumor?' and immediately challenges it.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading רב אשי's ruling as talking about a rumor after her remarriage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב אשי already stated that rule elsewhere, so saying it again would be needless repetition.
